description_full: DCC Energy plc engages in the sales, marketing, and distribution of carbon energy solutions in the Republic of Ireland, the United Kingdom, France, the United States, and internationally. The company operates in two segments, DCC Energy and DCC Technology. It sells transport and commercial fuels, heating oils and related products, liquid gas, refrigerants, electricity, natural gas; sells and distributes biofuels and biogas to commercial, industrial, and domestic customers; designs, sells, installs, and maintains on-site solar and energy systems for power customers, as well as provides energy efficiency solutions; owns or operates service stations (gas stations) for vehicles and trucks; and provides fleet payment, digital parking, and telematic services. The company also offers Pro Tech, which bring professional technologies together to enhance audio and visual experiences; Info Tech to make faster connections happen; and Life Tech that provides technology to improve lifestyle quality. The company was formerly known as DCC plc and changed its name to DCC Energy plc. in July 2026. The company was incorporated in 1976 and is headquartered in Dublin, Ireland.

financial_summary: DCC is a mid-cap energy business with a $7.3B market cap on $20.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $618M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 50.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 16.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 6.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
